name: Reverse-wrap cordage
summary: Two-ply cord twisted from plant fibre — the enabling material for shelter, traps, a bow drill and a pack.

substitutes: inner bark of basswood or cedar

steps.text: Collect stalks that have died and dried standing — dogbane and nettle in autumn, or the inner bark of a fallen basswood.
Crush the stalk and strip out the long outer fibres, then work them between your hands to break away the woody pith.
Take a bundle and twist it until it kinks and folds back on itself. That fold is the start.
Hold the fold. Twist the FAR strand away from you, then cross it over the near strand toward you. Repeat.
steps.why: The two plies are twisted one way and wrapped the other, so each ply's own tension locks the wrap. That opposition is the entire reason the cord holds.

steps.text: Splice in new fibre by feathering the ends and laying the new bundle into a ply about 3 cm before the old one runs out — never let both plies run out together.
For thicker cord, reverse-wrap two finished cords together the same way.

verify: The cord holds its twist when you let it go slack. If it unwinds, the plies were twisted too little before wrapping.
Splices should be invisible by feel — a lump is a weak point.
limits: Plant cordage is a fraction of the strength of manufactured line and degrades wet. Do not trust it with body weight.
Grass cord is weak and short-lived; use it for lashing, not for load.
cautions: Positively identify the plant before handling it in quantity — a great many fibre plants have irritant sap, and dogbane in particular is toxic if eaten.
Wet fibre is easier to work but the finished cord must be dried, or it rots.
